subject: rla
title: Analyzing Arguments: Claims, Evidence, Reasoning, and Faulty Reasoning
objectives: Students will identify an author's claim, reasons, counterclaim, and rebuttal in an argument.
Students will classify evidence and judge whether it is relevant, sufficient, and reliable.
Students will explain how reasoning connects evidence to a claim and identify unstated assumptions.
Students will recognize common types of faulty reasoning, including hasty generalization, false cause, slippery slope, either-or, and attack on the person.
Students will evaluate the credibility and relevance of sources by asking who wrote them, what evidence they give, when they were written, and why.
teach:
Lesson overview

Week 5 teaches learners to take an argument apart and judge how well it holds up. On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts (RLA) test, many reading questions are built on op-eds, letters, speeches, and position statements. Learners must find the author's claim, decide which evidence supports it, notice when reasoning goes wrong, and judge whether a source can be trusted. These same skills drive the extended response, where learners decide which of two arguments is better supported, so this week lays the foundation for Weeks 9 and 10.

Keep the tone neutral. The goal is never to decide which side of an issue is right; it is to decide which argument is better supported. Point out often that people on every side of every issue use both strong evidence and faulty reasoning.

Objectives

  • Identify an author's claim, reasons, counterclaim, and rebuttal.
  • Classify evidence and judge whether it is relevant, sufficient, and reliable.
  • Explain how reasoning connects evidence to a claim, and find unstated assumptions.
  • Recognize common types of faulty reasoning.
  • Evaluate the credibility of a source using four questions: Who, What, When, and Why.

Materials

  • Student Lesson (printed or on screen) and this week's Notes sheet
  • Whiteboard or shared screen; highlighters in three colors (claim, evidence, faulty reasoning)
  • Copies of the warm-up statements, worked examples, and guided-practice letter (all included below)
  • Week 5 practice items (the library op-ed, items 1–5, are used for independent practice)
  • Index cards or a shared document for the exit ticket

60-minute timing plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5“Which one convinces you?”: compare two short arguments
Direct instruction20Parts of an argument; types and tests of evidence; reasoning and assumptions; faulty reasoning; credibility; worked examples
Guided practice15Whole-group reading of a short letter, five questions
Independent practice15Practice items 1–5 (library op-ed); circulate and coach
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; exit ticket; assign the week's study plan

Warm-up (5 minutes): Which one convinces you?

Display both statements. Ask learners which is more convincing and to name one specific reason.

Statement A: We need a fenced dog park downtown. Everybody knows dogs need exercise, and anyone who disagrees just doesn't like dogs.

Statement B: We need a fenced dog park downtown. The city licensing office reports 2,300 licensed dogs within one mile of Main Street, and the nearest fenced dog area is four miles away.

Answer: Statement B. It gives specific numbers from a named source that a reader could check, and the numbers connect directly to the claim (many dogs, no nearby park). Statement A relies on “everybody knows,” which is not evidence, and it insults people who disagree instead of answering them. Tell learners: “You do not have to agree with a claim to see that it is well supported, and you do not have to disagree with a claim to see that it is poorly supported.”

Direct instruction (20 minutes)

Talking point 1: The parts of an argument (4 minutes)

Say: “An argument is a piece of writing that tries to convince you to believe or do something.” Draw this on the board:

PartQuestion it answers
ClaimWhat does the author want me to believe or do?
ReasonsWhy, according to the author?
EvidenceWhat facts, numbers, examples, or expert statements back up each reason?
ReasoningHow does the evidence prove the claim?
CounterclaimWhat does the other side say?
RebuttalHow does the author answer the other side?

Stress that the claim is usually stated near the beginning and repeated near the end, and that it is something people could reasonably disagree with. “Libraries lend books” is a fact. “Our library should stop charging late fines” is a claim.

Talking point 2: Evidence and the three tests (4 minutes)

List the common types: statistics, research findings, expert testimony, examples or comparable cases, anecdotes (personal stories), and personal observation. Then teach the three tests:

  • Relevant: Does it actually relate to this claim? A true fact about the wrong subject does not help.
  • Sufficient: Is there enough of it? One story or one small example is rarely enough to prove a general claim.
  • Reliable: Where did it come from? Could a reader check it? Was it gathered fairly?

Point out that anecdotes are not “wrong”; they make an argument vivid. But an anecdote alone is weak support for a claim about a whole town or a whole group.

Talking point 3: Reasoning and assumptions (3 minutes)

Say: “Reasoning is the bridge between the evidence and the claim. An assumption is a part of the bridge the author does not say out loud.” Example: “Westbrook sold more pool passes after it added evening hours, so we should add evening hours too.” The unstated assumption is that our town is similar enough to Westbrook for the same result to happen here. If the assumption is shaky, the argument is shaky.

Talking point 4: Faulty reasoning (6 minutes)

Faulty reasoning (also called a logical fallacy) is a flaw in the logic that makes an argument seem stronger than it is. Walk through this table, asking learners for an everyday example of each.

TypeWhat it doesAsk yourself
Hasty generalizationDraws a big conclusion from too few examplesIs this enough evidence to cover everyone?
False causeAssumes that because B happened after A, A caused BCould something else explain it?
Slippery slopeClaims one step will lead to a chain of disasters, without proofIs each step in the chain actually supported?
Either-or (false dilemma)Offers only two choices when more existAre these really the only options?
Attack on the person (ad hominem)Criticizes the people on the other side instead of their reasonsDid the author answer the argument or insult the arguer?
BandwagonSays something is right because many people believe or do itIs popularity the same as proof?
Straw manTwists the other side's view into a weaker version that is easy to knock downIs that what the other side actually said?
Loaded language / appeal to emotionUses strong feelings in place of evidenceOnce I remove the emotional words, what proof is left?

Tell learners that the GED rarely asks for the name of a fallacy. It asks which statement is not supported, which reasoning is flawed, or which evidence is weakest. Knowing the patterns helps them spot the flaw quickly.

Talking point 5: Credibility of sources (3 minutes)

Teach the four questions: Who wrote it, and do they have expertise? What evidence do they give, and could it be checked? When was it written, and is it current for this question? Why was it written, and does the author gain anything if readers agree? A source with a personal or financial stake is not automatically wrong, but readers should look harder at its evidence.

Worked examples

Example 1: Claim, evidence, reasoning.

“Our town should keep the public pool open until 8 p.m. on summer weekdays instead of closing at 6. Many residents work until 5 or later and cannot reach the pool before it closes. Last summer, the recreation department surveyed 900 pool pass holders, and 64 percent said they would swim more often if evening hours were added. Neighboring Westbrook extended its hours two years ago and sold 20 percent more season passes the following summer, which helped pay for the extra lifeguard shifts.”

Solution. Step 1: Claim: the pool should stay open until 8 p.m. on summer weekdays. Step 2: Reason: many residents cannot get there before 6. Step 3: Evidence: a survey of 900 pass holders (statistics from a named source) and the Westbrook result (a comparable case). Step 4: Reasoning: more people would swim, and higher pass sales could pay for the added staff. Step 5: Unstated assumption: our town is similar enough to Westbrook that pass sales would rise here too. Step 6: Judge it: the evidence is relevant and fairly strong, but the author never gives the actual cost of the extra shifts, so the money part is not fully supported.

Example 2: Name the flaw. Read each statement and identify the faulty reasoning.

  1. “Ever since the new coffee shop opened downtown, speeding tickets have gone up. That coffee shop is causing reckless driving.”
  2. “If we let seniors leave campus for lunch, next they will want to leave for whole afternoons, and soon no one will be in class.”
  3. “Ms. Park says the town should add bike lanes, but she can't even keep her own yard tidy.”
  4. “Either we raise the library budget, or our children will grow up unable to read.”
  5. “My cousin's car was broken into downtown, so downtown is not safe.”
  6. “People who oppose the youth curfew want teenagers roaming the streets all night with no rules at all.”

Solution. (1) False cause: tickets rose after the shop opened, but more traffic, more patrols, or many other factors could explain it. (2) Slippery slope: no evidence that one lunch policy leads to empty classrooms. (3) Attack on the person: her yard has nothing to do with whether bike lanes are a good idea. (4) Either-or: there are many ways to support reading besides this one budget. (5) Hasty generalization: one break-in cannot show that a whole area is unsafe. (6) Straw man: curfew opponents may want different rules or later hours, not “no rules at all.”

Point out that these examples come from many different positions. Faulty reasoning is a habit of thinking, not a feature of one side.

Example 3: Judge credibility. A reader wants to know whether standing desks reduce back pain for office workers. Which source is most credible?

  • Source 1: A standing-desk company's website, 2025: “Our customers report 90 percent less back pain!”
  • Source 2: A 2023 study in a medical journal. University researchers followed 400 office workers for one year, comparing workers who used standing desks with workers who did not.
  • Source 3: A 2008 magazine article about office furniture trends.
  • Source 4: A video by a fitness personality who says standing desks “changed my life.”

Solution. Apply Who, What, When, Why. Source 1: the company profits from sales (Why), and “customers report” is not a fair study (What). Source 2: trained researchers (Who), a large group compared with a control group over a year (What), recent (When), published to share findings (Why). Source 3: old, and about trends, not health. Source 4: one person's experience. Source 2 is most credible.

Example 4: Strengthen or weaken. Claim: “The town should replace downtown parking meters with free two-hour parking because free parking will bring more shoppers to downtown stores.”

Which fact would strengthen it? Which would weaken it?

(a) In three nearby towns that removed their meters, downtown store sales rose the next year. (b) In a survey of downtown shoppers, most said their biggest problem was finding an open space, not paying for one.

Solution. (a) strengthens the claim: it shows the expected result happening in comparable places. (b) weakens it: if cost is not what keeps shoppers away, free parking may not bring more of them, and it could make open spaces even harder to find.

Guided practice (15 minutes)

Read this letter aloud together. Learners highlight the claim in one color, evidence in another, and faulty reasoning in a third. Then discuss the questions.

Bring the Farmers Market to Sundays

(1) The town should add a Sunday farmers market from June through September. (2) Right now the market runs only on Saturday mornings, when many residents are working. (3) Last fall, the market association surveyed its 42 vendors, and 30 of them said they would sell on Sundays as well. (4) The nearby town of Oakdale added a Sunday market three years ago, and it now draws about 1,500 shoppers each week. (5) Some people say a second market day will split the crowd and hurt Saturday sales. (6) But Oakdale's Saturday attendance has stayed steady since its Sunday market opened. (7) Besides, every town worth living in has a Sunday market these days.

  1. What is the writer's claim? Answer: The town should add a Sunday farmers market from June through September (sentence 1).
  2. Which sentence gives a counterclaim, and which gives the rebuttal? Answer: Sentence 5 is the counterclaim (a second day will hurt Saturday sales). Sentence 6 is the rebuttal (Oakdale's Saturday attendance stayed steady).
  3. What type of evidence is sentence 3? Is it relevant? Answer: Statistics from a survey. It is relevant because a market needs vendors willing to sell on Sunday.
  4. Which sentence uses faulty reasoning, and what kind? Answer: Sentence 7. It is a bandwagon appeal (and loaded language, “worth living in”). It gives no evidence, only a claim that “everyone” does it.
  5. What assumption connects sentences 4 and 6 to the claim? Answer: That this town is similar enough to Oakdale for the same results to happen here.

Independent practice (15 minutes)

Learners complete practice items 1–5 on the library op-ed. Circulate. When a learner is stuck, ask: “What does the author want? What proves it? Could a reader check that proof?”

Checks for understanding

  • “What is the difference between a claim and evidence?” Expected: A claim is what the author wants you to believe or do; evidence is the facts, numbers, examples, or expert statements that back it up.
  • “Why is one personal story weak support for a claim about a whole town?” Expected: It is not sufficient; one case may not represent what usually happens.
  • “Something happened after a change. Does that prove the change caused it?” Expected: No. That is false cause; other factors may explain it.
  • “Name the four credibility questions.” Expected: Who, What, When, Why.
  • “What is a rebuttal?” Expected: The author's answer to the other side's argument.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

  • Picking a statistic as the claim. Learners see a striking number and call it the main point. Ask: “Is this what the author wants us to do, or proof of it?”
  • Thinking numbers always mean strong evidence. A poll of 150 self-selected people is a number, but it is not reliable. Ask how the number was gathered.
  • Choosing the answer they agree with. Remind learners that the question is about support, not opinion. Have them argue the side they disagree with for one minute.
  • Calling every emotional sentence faulty. Emotion becomes a flaw only when it replaces evidence. A moving story next to solid data is fine.
  • Trusting a credible source that is off topic. Expert research about other cities does not prove what happened on one street. Credible and relevant are two separate tests.

Differentiation

Support: Give learners a sentence-sorting card set (claim, evidence, counterclaim, rebuttal) for the farmers market letter before they read it as a paragraph. Limit the fallacy list to four (hasty generalization, false cause, either-or, attack on the person) for the first pass. Pair learners to read the op-ed aloud.

Stretch: Have learners rewrite a flawed sentence from the skate park letter (practice items 6–8) so that it uses relevant evidence instead of faulty reasoning. Ask them to write a counterclaim and rebuttal for the library op-ed from the opposing view, using only reasonable evidence.

How this shows up on the GED

Expect argument passages such as op-eds, letters to the editor, speeches, and position papers, sometimes paired. Typical wording includes:

  • “Which statement best expresses the author's claim?”
  • “Which evidence from the passage best supports the claim that …?”
  • “Which claim in the passage is not supported by evidence?”
  • “How does the author respond to the counterclaim in paragraph 3?”
  • “Which statement, if true, would most weaken the author's argument?”
  • “Why is the evidence in paragraph 4 less convincing than the evidence in paragraph 2?”

Formats include multiple choice, drag-and-drop sorting of claims and evidence, clicking the sentence that contains flawed reasoning, and drop-down menus inside editing passages that ask for the most relevant supporting sentence or the right transition before a rebuttal. These skills also power the extended response, where learners must explain which of two arguments is better supported.
student:
Why this skill matters

Every day, people try to convince you of something: a letter to the editor, a campaign flyer, an ad, a post from a neighbor. On the GED Reasoning Through Language Arts test, you will read arguments like these and answer questions about how well they hold up. You do not need to agree or disagree with the author. Your job is to decide whether the author proves the point. This week you will learn to find the claim, judge the evidence, spot faulty reasoning, and decide whether a source can be trusted.

The parts of an argument

PartWhat it isExample
ClaimWhat the author wants you to believe or doThe city should add evening hours at the pool.
ReasonWhy the author thinks soMany residents work until 5 or later.
EvidenceFacts, numbers, examples, or expert statements that back up a reasonIn a survey of 900 pass holders, 64 percent wanted evening hours.
CounterclaimThe other side's positionSome say longer hours cost too much.
RebuttalThe author's answer to the other sideExtra pass sales in a nearby town covered the added cost.

Quick check: A claim is something reasonable people could disagree about. “The pool closes at 6” is a fact. “The pool should close at 8” is a claim.

Judging evidence: three tests

Evidence comes in many forms: statistics, research studies, expert statements, comparable cases (what happened somewhere else), personal stories (anecdotes), and personal observations. Test every piece of evidence three ways.

  1. Relevant: Is it actually about this claim? A true fact on a different subject does not help.
  2. Sufficient: Is there enough? One story cannot prove what is true for a whole town.
  3. Reliable: Where did it come from, and was it gathered fairly? Could you check it?

Stories and observations make an argument easy to picture, but they are usually the weakest kind of support. Data from a named, trustworthy source that covers many people is usually the strongest.

Reasoning and assumptions

Reasoning is the link between the evidence and the claim. An assumption is a link the author does not state but needs you to accept. If an author writes, “A nearby town added a Sunday market and drew 1,500 shoppers, so we should too,” the hidden assumption is that our town is similar enough to that town. When an assumption is doubtful, the argument is weaker.

Faulty reasoning

Faulty reasoning makes an argument sound stronger than it is. Learn to recognize these patterns.

TypeWhat it looks like
Hasty generalization“I saw two drivers run that light, so everyone on this street drives recklessly.”
False cause“Crime went up the year the mall opened, so the mall caused it.”
Slippery slope“If we allow food trucks this summer, soon the whole downtown will be nothing but food trucks.”
Either-or“Either we build a new school or our kids get no education.”
Attack on the person“Don't listen to his plan for the parks. He doesn't even own a house here.”
Bandwagon“Everyone is switching to this plan, so it must be the right choice.”
Straw man“My opponents want to get rid of all rules.” (when they only asked to change one)
Appeal to emotionStrong feelings or loaded words used instead of evidence

The GED usually does not ask you to name the fallacy. It asks which statement is not supported or which reasoning is flawed. Ask yourself: “Does the proof really lead to this conclusion?”

Judging a source: Who, What, When, Why

  • Who wrote it? Does the person or group have real knowledge of the subject?
  • What evidence does it give? Data and methods you could check, or just opinions?
  • When was it written? Is it current enough for the question you are asking?
  • Why was it written? Does the author gain money, votes, or customers if you agree?

A source with something to gain is not automatically wrong. It just means you should look harder at its evidence.

Worked examples

Example 1: Find the parts. “The library should open on Sunday afternoons. Many students work on Saturdays and have no quiet place to study on weekends. When the library tested Sunday hours last spring, an average of 210 people came each Sunday. Some say the library cannot afford more hours, but the library director reports that a literacy grant already covers the cost of staff for those hours.”

Step 1. Claim: the library should open on Sunday afternoons.
Step 2. Reason: students have no quiet weekend study space.
Step 3. Evidence: 210 people per Sunday during a trial.
Step 4. Counterclaim: the library cannot afford it.
Step 5. Rebuttal: a grant already covers the cost, according to the director.

Example 2: Spot the flaw. “Our town started allowing scooter rentals in April, and in May, two people sprained their ankles downtown. Scooters are making our streets dangerous.”

Step 1. What is the conclusion? Scooters are making streets dangerous.
Step 2. What is the proof? Two sprained ankles in the month after rentals began.
Step 3. Does the proof lead to the conclusion? No. The writer never says the injuries involved scooters. This is false cause (and two cases is too few to show a pattern).

Example 3: Judge two sources. Question: Did the town's new recycling program reduce trash sent to the landfill?

Source A: A newsletter from the company that won the recycling contract: “Our program is a huge success!”
Source B: The town's public works report with landfill weights for the two years before and the two years after the program began.

Step 1. Who and Why: the company profits from the contract, so it has a stake in calling the program a success. The town department tracks landfill weights as part of its job.
Step 2. What: Source A gives no numbers. Source B gives measured weights that can be compared.
Step 3. Source B is more credible.

Try it

1. “We should repaint the crosswalks near the elementary school this summer. The paint has faded so much that drivers cannot see the lines.” Which sentence is the claim?

Show answer

The first sentence: “We should repaint the crosswalks near the elementary school this summer.” The second sentence is the reason.

2. “Anyone who supports the new bus route clearly hasn't thought about our taxes.” What is wrong with this reasoning?

Show answer

It attacks the people on the other side instead of giving evidence about the bus route. It also assumes, without proof, that supporters have not considered taxes. This is an attack on the person.

3. A writer argues that a new diet plan works because “over a million people have already signed up.” What kind of faulty reasoning is this?

Show answer

Bandwagon. The number of people who signed up says nothing about whether the plan works.

4. You want to know whether a new medicine is safe. Which is more credible: a 2024 study by independent researchers that tracked 2,000 patients, or an ad from the company that makes the medicine? Why?

Show answer

The independent study. The researchers do not profit from sales (Why), they tracked a large number of patients (What), and the study is recent (When). The company has a financial stake and an ad is designed to sell.

5. “Either we cut the summer reading program or we raise property taxes.” What question should you ask?

Show answer

“Are these really the only two choices?” There may be other options, such as grants, donations, or cuts elsewhere. This is an either-or (false dilemma).
post:
Summary of key points

  • An argument has a claim (what the author wants), reasons, evidence, and reasoning that ties them together. Strong arguments also answer a counterclaim with a rebuttal.
  • Test evidence three ways: relevant, sufficient, and reliable.
  • Look for unstated assumptions; a shaky assumption weakens the whole argument.
  • Watch for faulty reasoning: hasty generalization, false cause, slippery slope, either-or, attack on the person, bandwagon, straw man, and emotion used in place of evidence.
  • Judge sources with Who, What, When, Why. A source can be credible but still not relevant to your question.
  • Your job is to judge support, not to pick the side you agree with.

Exit ticket

1. Is “The town should ban leaf blowers before 8 a.m.” a fact or a claim? Explain.

Show answer

A claim. It says what should happen, and people could reasonably disagree.

2. Name the three tests for evidence.

Show answer

Relevant, sufficient, and reliable.

3. “After the town painted the bridge blue, fewer people visited the park. The color drove visitors away.” What is the flaw?

Show answer

False cause. The drop in visitors came after the painting, but the writer gives no proof that the color caused it. Weather, road work, or other events could explain it.

4. What is the difference between a counterclaim and a rebuttal?

Show answer

A counterclaim is the other side's position. A rebuttal is the author's answer to it.

5. A website selling water filters says tap water in every city is dangerous. Which credibility question raises the biggest concern?

Show answer

Why. The company profits if readers believe tap water is unsafe. (What is also a concern: “every city” is a broad claim that would need strong data.)

Reflection

  • Think of an argument you heard this week, on the news, at work, or online. What was the claim, and how strong was the evidence?
  • Which type of faulty reasoning do you think you hear most often? Why do you think it works on people?
  • Was it harder to judge an argument you agreed with or one you disagreed with? Why?

DayWhat to doTime
Day 1Reread the Student Lesson. Redo the Try it problems without looking at the answers.25 min
Day 2Study the vocabulary. Find one letter to the editor or opinion piece and label its claim, two pieces of evidence, and any counterclaim.25 min
Day 3Complete practice items 1–6. Read every explanation, even for items you got right.30 min
Day 4Complete practice items 7–12. For each miss, write which test (relevant, sufficient, reliable) or which flaw you overlooked.30 min
Day 5Flaw hunt: find three examples of faulty reasoning in ads, posts, or conversations. Rewrite one so it uses real evidence.25 min
Day 6Take this week's Practice GED for Reasoning Through Language Arts under timed conditions.40 min, continue on Day 7 if needed
Day 7Finish the Practice GED if needed. Review every missed question and list the skills to work on.30 min

Test-taking strategy: Cover the opinion, check the proof

On an argument question, set your own opinion aside. Find the claim first, then ask of every answer choice: “Can I point to the place in the passage that proves this?” If a choice sounds right but you cannot point to proof, or the proof is a single story, a popularity count, or an insult, it is probably the wrong answer or the weak evidence the question is asking about.

vocab.def: A piece of writing or speech that tries to convince the reader to believe or do something.
vocab.example: A letter urging the council to build a new bus shelter.

vocab.def: The main position an author wants readers to accept; something reasonable people could disagree about.
vocab.example: The library should stop charging late fines.

vocab.def: Facts, statistics, research, expert statements, or examples used to support a claim.
vocab.example: Fines brought in $21,500, less than 1 percent of the budget.

vocab.def: The logic that explains how the evidence proves the claim.
vocab.example: Return rates stayed the same without fines, so fines are not what gets books returned.

vocab.def: An idea the author takes for granted without stating it, which the argument depends on.
vocab.example: Assuming our town will respond the same way a nearby town did.

vocab.def: A position that opposes the author's claim.
The author's response that answers or disproves a counterclaim.
vocab.example: But return rates barely changed when another library dropped fines.

vocab.def: Evidence that is directly connected to the claim it is meant to support.
vocab.example: Crash data from the street in question, not from a different city.

vocab.def: Enough evidence to support the size of the claim being made.
vocab.example: One story is not sufficient to describe a whole town.

vocab.def: How trustworthy and believable a source is, based on its expertise, evidence, date, and purpose.
vocab.example: A peer-reviewed study is usually more credible than an online comment.

vocab.def: A leaning toward one side, often because the author has something to gain or a strong personal view.
vocab.example: A shop owner praising a project that brings customers to the shop.

vocab.def: A flaw in logic that makes an argument seem stronger than it really is.
vocab.example: Insulting the other side instead of answering it.

vocab.def: A broad conclusion drawn from too few examples.
vocab.example: Two teens littered, so all skaters will ruin the park.

vocab.def: Assuming that because one event followed another, the first event caused the second.
vocab.example: Break-ins rose after the skate park opened, so the skate park caused them.

vocab.def: Claiming, without proof, that one step will lead to a chain of increasingly bad results.
vocab.example: Allow a skate park, and soon the whole park will be paved.

notes:
Week 5 RLA Study Sheet: Analyzing Arguments

Parts of an argument

  • Claim: what the author wants you to believe or do
  • Reason: why the author thinks so
  • Evidence: facts, numbers, studies, expert statements, examples
  • Reasoning: how the evidence proves the claim
  • Assumption: an unstated link the author needs you to accept
  • Counterclaim: the other side's view
  • Rebuttal: the author's answer to it

Three tests for evidence

  1. Relevant: about this claim?
  2. Sufficient: enough to cover the claim?
  3. Reliable: trustworthy, fairly gathered, checkable?

Strongest: data from a named, fair source. Weakest: one story, a self-selected poll, “everyone knows.”

Source credibility

  • Who: expertise?
  • What: data and methods, or opinion?
  • When: current for this question?
  • Why: does the author gain if you agree?

Credible is not the same as relevant. Check both.

Strengthen or weaken?

Strengthens: new evidence that makes the claim more likely. Weakens: evidence that breaks the link between proof and claim.

Faulty reasoning

TypeSignAsk yourself
Hasty generalizationBig conclusion, few casesEnough examples?
False causeB came after A, so A caused BOther explanations?
Slippery slopeOne step leads to disasterIs each step proven?
Either-orOnly two choicesOther options?
Attack on the personInsults the arguerWere the reasons answered?
BandwagonEveryone thinks soPopular = proven?
Straw manTwists the other side's viewDid they really say that?
Appeal to emotionFeelings replace factsWhat proof is left?

Strategy: Set your opinion aside. Find the claim, then point to the proof for each answer choice.

Common mistakes: calling a statistic the claim; trusting any number; choosing the side you agree with; trusting a credible but off-topic source.

stimuli.title: Fines Don't Bring the Books Back
stimuli.html:
An opinion column by Dana Whitfield, a retired school librarian who volunteers with the Friends of the Brookdale Library

(1) Right now, 1,240 Brookdale residents cannot borrow a single book from their public library. Their cards are blocked because each of them owes more than $10 in late fines. That is about one of every nine active library cards in town. Next month, the library board will vote on whether to stop charging fines for overdue materials. The board should vote yes. Late fines do little to get books returned, they raise very little money, and they push away the very people a public library is meant to serve.

(2) Supporters of fines argue that the charges teach responsibility and give borrowers a reason to return items on time. It is a fair concern, but the evidence does not back it up. When the Lakeview County Library stopped charging late fines in 2021, it tracked what happened next. Before the change, 92 percent of borrowed items came back within one week of their due date. Two years after the change, the figure was 91 percent, nearly the same. Under the plan before the Brookdale board, borrowers who keep an item more than a month past its due date would still be billed for its replacement cost, and their cards would be blocked until the item is returned or paid for. People would still have every reason to bring books back. They simply would not be charged a growing daily penalty for being a few days late.

(3) Some board members worry that the library cannot afford to give up the money. The numbers say otherwise. Last year, fines brought in $21,500, which is less than 1 percent of the library's $2.6 million budget. Collecting that money is not free, either. Library director Marisol Grant estimates that staff members spend about 600 hours a year collecting fines, processing payments, and settling disputes over charges. At the library's average staff wage of $22 an hour, that time costs about $13,200. Once that cost is subtracted, fines bring in only about $8,300 a year, and those 600 hours could be spent helping patrons instead.

(4) The real cost of fines falls on the people who can least afford them. According to the library's own records, more than half of the blocked cards belong to children and teenagers, who often have no way to pay a fine themselves. Last spring, I stood behind a mother at the checkout desk who had to put back the picture books her six-year-old son had chosen because she could not pay a $14 balance. He left with nothing. When Lakeview dropped its fines, more than 3,100 residents whose cards had been blocked came back and began borrowing again within the first year.

(5) Residents clearly want this change. In an online poll on a neighborhood message board last month, 80 percent of the 150 people who responded said the library should go fine-free.

(6) Ending late fines will not solve every challenge the library faces. But the evidence shows that it would reopen the library to more than a thousand residents while costing the library very little. A library's job is to put books into people's hands, not to keep them out. The board should vote yes.

stimuli.title: Letter to the Editor: Keep the East Lawn Open
stimuli.html:
To the Editor:

(1) On March 12, the town council will vote on a plan to build a skate park on the east lawn of Fairview Park. I have lived on Linden Street, across from the park, for thirty-one years, and I urge the council to vote no.

(2) First, consider the cost. According to the parks department's own estimate, the skate park would cost $310,000 to build and about $12,000 a year to maintain. That is a significant amount of money for a town of our size, and the council has not explained where it would come from.

(3) Second, a skate park would bring trouble. Last Saturday, I watched two teenagers on skateboards toss soda cans into the bushes by the playground. If that is how skaters treat the park now, imagine how they will treat a park built just for them. Look at what happened in Cedar Hills. That town opened a skate park in 2019, and the next year car break-ins there went up. Clearly, the skate park caused it.

(4) Third, the skate park would take space that many people already use. On summer weekends, the east lawn is full of families having picnics and children playing pickup soccer. If we approve a skate park this year, next year skaters will demand lights, then a snack stand, then a parking lot, and before long the whole park will be paved over. The council should protect the lawn for the many residents who enjoy it now.

(5) Fourth, the people pushing this project hardly represent the town. Most of them moved here in the last few years and do not understand what Fairview Park means to the families who have been here for generations. Meanwhile, everyone I have talked to on my street is against the plan.

(6) Finally, the council needs to set priorities. The choice is simple: either we spend $310,000 on a skate park, or we fix the potholes on Main Street. We cannot do both.

(7) Fairview Park belongs to all of us. I ask the council to keep it that way and vote no.

Gordon Pell
Linden Street

stimuli.title: Draft Letter: We Need a Safe Crossing on Oak Street
stimuli.html:
To the Editor:

(1) The town should install a marked crosswalk with a flashing pedestrian signal where Oak Street meets Fifth Avenue. Every day, hundreds of people cross Oak Street at this corner to reach the senior center, the Route 4 bus stop, and Grover's Market. Right now, they have no crosswalk, no signal, and no stop sign to slow drivers down.

(2) This crossing is dangerous. (A) Two of those crashes sent pedestrians to the hospital. Most of the people who were hurt were walking to or from the senior center.

(3) Some residents argue that a signal would slow traffic on one of the town's busiest streets. (B) the town's traffic engineer estimates that the signal would add less than 30 seconds to the average drive along Oak Street. That is a small price for a safer crossing.

(4) Cost is not a barrier, either. A similar signal installed at Maple Street last year cost about $45,000, and the town already has money set aside in (C) road safety fund for exactly this kind of project.

(5) I urge the council to act before anyone else is hurt.

Lena Ortiz
Fifth Avenue

stimuli.title: Sources on the Elm Street Bike Lane
stimuli.html:
A student is researching this question: Did the protected bike lane that opened on Elm Street in Riverton in 2021 make Elm Street safer? The student found these five sources.

SourceAuthor and dateWhat it says
ARiverton Department of Transportation, “Elm Street Safety Review,” 2025Compares police crash reports on Elm Street for the three years before the lane opened (2018–2020) and the three years after (2022–2024). Total crashes fell from 47 to 29; crashes involving cyclists fell from 11 to 6. Full data tables and methods are included.
BBlog post by the owner of a bicycle shop on Elm Street, 2024“The new lane has made Elm Street the safest street in the city. Business has never been better!” No data are given.
CArticle in a peer-reviewed transportation research journal by university researchers, 2023Studied protected bike lanes in 12 cities and found that crashes fell by an average of 30 percent on streets after protected lanes were added. Riverton was not one of the 12 cities.
DComment by a resident in a neighborhood social media group, 2025“I nearly got hit by a cyclist on Elm last week. These lanes are a disaster.”
ENewspaper article, 2012Quotes a city planner predicting that a protected bike lane on Elm Street, then under discussion, “will cut crashes in half.”

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the author's claim in the op-ed?
options: The library board should vote to stop charging late fines on overdue materials.
About one of every nine active library cards in Brookdale is currently blocked.
Late fines teach borrowers to be responsible and return items on time.
The library should cut staff hours to make up for the money it loses from fines.
items.hint: Look for what the author wants the board to do. She states it in paragraph 1 and repeats it at the end.
items.explain:
Step 1. A claim is what the author wants readers to believe or do. Check paragraph 1 and the conclusion: “The board should vote yes” on whether to stop charging fines for overdue materials. She repeats this in paragraph 6.

Step 2. “The library board should vote to stop charging late fines” matches. Correct.

Step 3. Check the traps. The one-in-nine figure is evidence the author uses, not her claim. “Fines teach responsibility” is the counterclaim she argues against in paragraph 2. Cutting staff hours is never suggested; in fact, she says the 600 hours could go to helping patrons.

items.prompt: What kind of evidence does the author use in paragraph 2 to respond to people who say fines get books returned on time?
options: Statistics comparing return rates at another library before and after it ended fines
A personal story about a family at the library checkout desk
A quotation from an expert who studies library budgets
The results of an online poll of local residents
items.hint: Reread paragraph 2 and look at the numbers. Where do they come from, and what do they compare?
items.explain:
Step 1. Paragraph 2 reports that at the Lakeview County Library, 92 percent of items came back within a week before fines ended and 91 percent two years after.

Step 2. These are statistics comparing return rates before and after a change at another library. Correct.

Step 3. The personal story about the mother and son is in paragraph 4, and the online poll is in paragraph 5, so they are not used in paragraph 2. No expert on library budgets is quoted anywhere; the director's estimate in paragraph 3 is about staff hours.

items.prompt: The author claims that ending late fines would cost the library very little. Which two details best support this part of her argument? Select two answers.
options: Fines brought in $21,500 last year, which is less than 1 percent of the library's $2.6 million budget.
Staff spend about 600 hours a year handling fines, time worth about $13,200 in wages.
More than half of the blocked cards belong to children and teenagers.
At Lakeview, 92 percent of items were returned within a week before fines ended, and 91 percent after.
Eighty percent of 150 people who answered an online poll said the library should go fine-free.
About 1,240 residents currently have blocked library cards.
items.hint: The question is about money. Which details mention dollars the library would lose or save?
items.explain:
Step 1. Identify the part of the argument: ending fines would cost the library very little. Relevant evidence must be about money.

Step 2. Fines are less than 1 percent of the budget (paragraph 3): the lost income is small. Correct. Collecting fines takes about 600 staff hours worth about $13,200, so the library keeps only about $8,300 ($21,500 − $13,200 = $8,300). Correct.

Step 3. The other details are real evidence from the op-ed, but they support different points: who is hurt by fines (children and teenagers, blocked cards), whether books still come back (Lakeview return rates), or public opinion (the poll). None of them is about cost.

items.prompt: How does the author respond to the counterclaim that fines teach responsibility and get items returned on time?
options: She calls it a fair concern, then shows that return rates at a library without fines stayed nearly the same.
She argues that responsibility should be taught at home rather than by the library.
She points out that more than half of the blocked cards belong to children and teenagers.
She suggests that people who support fines rarely use the library themselves.
items.hint: Find the paragraph where the counterclaim appears. What does the author say right after it?
items.explain:
Step 1. The counterclaim appears at the start of paragraph 2: “Supporters of fines argue that the charges teach responsibility and give borrowers a reason to return items on time.”

Step 2. The next sentences are the rebuttal: “It is a fair concern, but the evidence does not back it up,” followed by Lakeview's return rates (92 percent before, 91 percent after). Correct.

Step 3. The author never mentions teaching responsibility at home. The children-and-teenagers detail is from paragraph 4 and supports a different point (who is hurt by fines). She never attacks supporters of fines personally; that would be faulty reasoning, and it is not in the text.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, the author states that “residents clearly want this change.” Why does the evidence she gives provide weak support for this statement?
options: The poll counted only 150 people who chose to answer on a message board, so they may not represent most residents.
The poll was taken last month, so its results are already out of date.
Eighty percent is too small a share to show that people support a change.
The poll asked about late fines instead of asking about the library's budget.
items.hint: Think about who answered the poll and how they were chosen.
items.explain:
Step 1. The claim is broad: residents clearly want the change. The proof is one online poll with 150 responses on a neighborhood message board.

Step 2. The people who answered chose themselves; they are people who use that message board and cared enough to respond. That small, self-selected group may not represent the town. The evidence is not sufficient or reliable for such a broad claim. Correct.

Step 3. Last month is recent, so timing is not the problem. Eighty percent is a large majority, not a small share. Asking about late fines is exactly the relevant question; the budget is a different issue.

items.prompt: Paragraph 4 of the letter is shown below. Click the sentence that claims, without evidence, that one decision will lead to a chain of worse and worse results.
spans: Third, the skate park would take space that many people already use.
On summer weekends, the east lawn is full of families having picnics and children playing pickup soccer.
If we approve a skate park this year, next year skaters will demand lights, then a snack stand, then a parking lot, and before long the whole park will be paved over.
The council should protect the lawn for the many residents who enjoy it now.
items.hint: Look for a sentence that moves step by step from one event to bigger and bigger consequences.
items.explain:
Step 1. The prompt describes a slippery slope: one step is said to lead to a chain of increasingly bad results, with no proof for each step.

Step 2. “If we approve a skate park this year, next year skaters will demand lights, then a snack stand, then a parking lot, and before long the whole park will be paved over.” The writer offers no evidence that any of these later steps would happen. Correct.

Step 3. The first sentence is the paragraph's reason (topic sentence). The second is the writer's observation of how the lawn is used, which is relevant support. The last sentence restates what the writer wants the council to do.

items.prompt: Drag each statement from the letter into the category that best describes its reasoning.
choices: Last Saturday, I watched two teenagers on skateboards toss soda cans into the bushes. If that is how skaters treat the park now, imagine how they will treat a park built just for them.
That town opened a skate park in 2019, and the next year car break-ins there went up. Clearly, the skate park caused it.
Either we spend $310,000 on a skate park, or we fix the potholes on Main Street. We cannot do both.
According to the parks department's own estimate, the skate park would cost $310,000 to build and about $12,000 a year to maintain.
On summer weekends, the east lawn is full of families having picnics and children playing pickup soccer.
items.hint: Ask of each statement: Is the conclusion based on too few cases? On timing alone? On only two choices? Or on relevant facts the writer could reasonably know?
items.explain:
Hasty generalization: The writer saw two teenagers litter once and concludes how all skaters will treat a skate park. Two people on one day are too few to judge a whole group.

False cause: Break-ins in Cedar Hills rose the year after its skate park opened, but timing alone does not prove the skate park caused them. The writer gives no evidence linking the two.

Either-or: The writer offers only two choices, a skate park or pothole repair, without showing that the town's budget allows only one. Other options (different funding sources, a smaller design, phasing the work) are ignored.

Reasonable support: The cost figures come from a named, official source (the parks department) and are relevant to whether the town should spend the money. The description of families using the lawn is an observation from someone who has lived across from the park for thirty-one years, and it is relevant to the claim that the park would take away space people use.

items.prompt: Which sentence from the letter criticizes the people who support the skate park instead of responding to their reasons?
options: Most of them moved here in the last few years and do not understand what Fairview Park means to the families who have been here for generations.
That is a significant amount of money for a town of our size, and the council has not explained where it would come from.
On summer weekends, the east lawn is full of families having picnics and children playing pickup soccer.
The council should protect the lawn for the many residents who enjoy it now.
items.hint: Look for a sentence about the supporters themselves, not about the skate park.
items.explain:
Step 1. An attack on the person (ad hominem) judges an idea by criticizing the people who hold it.

Step 2. In paragraph 5, the writer dismisses supporters because they are newcomers who supposedly “do not understand” the park. How long someone has lived in town says nothing about whether a skate park is a good idea. Correct.

Step 3. The other sentences are about the issue itself: the cost and funding of the project, how the lawn is used now, and what the writer wants the council to do. Whether or not you agree with them, none of them targets the supporters personally.

items.prompt:
Read the draft letter. Then choose the option that correctly completes each blank in these excerpts.

Paragraph 2, blank (A): This crossing is dangerous. {{0}} Two of those crashes sent pedestrians to the hospital.

Paragraph 3, blank (B): Some residents argue that a signal would slow traffic on one of the town's busiest streets. {{1}} the town's traffic engineer estimates that the signal would add less than 30 seconds to the average drive along Oak Street.

Paragraph 4, blank (C): The town already has money set aside in {{2}} road safety fund for exactly this kind of project.

options: Police records show eleven crashes involving pedestrians at this intersection in the past three years.
Oak Street was first paved in 1958 and has been repaved twice since then.
My neighbor says the drivers in this town are the worst she has ever seen.
Crosswalks in most towns are painted with white reflective stripes.
However,
For example,
Similarly,
As a result,
its
it's
their
its'

items.hint: For (A), the next sentence says “Two of those crashes.” For (B), the sentence answers an objection. For (C), the word refers to “the town” and shows ownership.
items.explain:
Blank (A). Step 1: The topic sentence claims the crossing is dangerous, so the next sentence should give relevant, reliable evidence. Step 2: The following sentence refers to “those crashes,” so the missing sentence must mention crashes. Step 3: “Police records show eleven crashes involving pedestrians at this intersection in the past three years” is relevant, specific, and from a checkable source. Correct. The paving history and the color of crosswalks are not about danger. The neighbor's comment is one person's opinion about drivers in general, not evidence about this intersection.

Blank (B). Step 1: The first sentence states a counterclaim (a signal would slow traffic). Step 2: The next sentence answers it with contrasting evidence, so a contrast transition is needed: “However,” Correct. “For example” would introduce an example of slowed traffic; “Similarly” signals agreement; “As a result” signals cause and effect. None fits a rebuttal.

Blank (C). Step 1: The word refers to “the town,” which is singular, and shows that the fund belongs to the town. Step 2: The singular possessive pronoun is its, with no apostrophe. Correct. “It's” means “it is” (“in it is road safety fund” makes no sense). “Their” is plural and does not agree with “town.” “Its'” is not a word.

items.prompt: Which source gives the most credible and relevant evidence about whether the Elm Street lane itself made Elm Street safer?
options: Source A, the Riverton Department of Transportation's safety review
Source B, the blog post by the owner of a bicycle shop on Elm Street
Source C, the research article on protected bike lanes in 12 cities
Source D, the resident's comment in a social media group
items.hint: Use Who, What, When, Why, and remember that the question is about Elm Street specifically.
items.explain:
Step 1. The question is about one street: did this lane make Elm Street safer? The best source must be both credible and about Elm Street.

Step 2. Source A measures Elm Street crashes for three years before and three years after the lane, using police reports, and includes its data and methods so readers can check them (What). It is recent (When). Total crashes fell from 47 to 29. Correct. (A city reviewing its own project could have a stake in a good result, which is why its published data and methods matter.)

Step 3. Source C is credible research, but Riverton was not studied, so it is not direct evidence about Elm Street. Source B gives no data and the author has a business interest. Source D is one person's single experience.

items.prompt: Which statement best evaluates Sources C and E as evidence for the student's question?
options: Source C is careful research but does not include Elm Street, and Source E is a prediction made before the lane was built, so neither shows what actually happened on Elm Street.
Source C is not credible because it was written by university researchers instead of city officials, while Source E is credible because a city planner is an expert.
Source C is outdated because it was published before Source A, and Source E is the most reliable source because it was written first.
Both sources are biased because they agree that protected bike lanes reduce crashes.
items.hint: Check two things for each source: Is it trustworthy? Is it about what actually happened on Elm Street after 2021?
items.explain:
Step 1: Source C. It is peer-reviewed university research covering 12 cities, so it is credible. But Riverton was not one of the 12 cities, so it can only suggest what might happen on Elm Street. It is credible but only indirectly relevant.

Step 2: Source E. It was written in 2012, nine years before the lane opened, and it quotes a prediction. A prediction is not evidence of results.

Step 3. So neither source shows what actually happened on Elm Street. Correct.

Step 4. University researchers are not less credible than city officials. Being published before another source does not make research outdated, and an older prediction is less useful here, not more. Agreeing with each other is not the same as being biased; bias comes from a stake in the outcome or an unfair method.

items.prompt: Return to the library op-ed. Which statement, if true, would most weaken the author's argument?
options: At several libraries similar to Brookdale's, the share of items returned late rose sharply after late fines ended.
More than half of Brookdale's blocked library cards belong to children and teenagers.
Many libraries now lend e-books that disappear from a reader's device automatically on the due date.
Brookdale's library budget has grown by about 2 percent a year over the last ten years.
items.hint: Which of the author's key pieces of evidence could a new fact undercut? Look especially at paragraph 2.
items.explain:
Step 1. A central reason in the op-ed is that ending fines does not hurt return rates. Her only evidence is one library, Lakeview, where return rates barely changed. Her reasoning assumes Brookdale would see the same result.

Step 2. If several similar libraries saw late returns rise sharply, that assumption falls apart, and the counterclaim (fines get books returned) gains support. Correct.

Step 3. The children-and-teenagers fact already appears in the op-ed and supports the author. E-books return themselves, so they say nothing about whether physical books come back without fines. A growing budget does not weaken the argument; if anything, it makes the small loss of fine income even less important.
